- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then underestimates later.
- Forecasts tend to overshoot after sharp price spikes (e.g., 75–80 range), then sharply correct downward — model fails to capture this “rebound” or “mean reversion” effect.
- Model exhibits persistent downward bias in the final 10–15 days of the 30-day forecast, suggesting it underestimates downward momentum or fails to account for seasonal/structural decline.
- Model often fails to adjust for recent price volatility — e.g., after a spike, it continues to project high values instead of trending down.
- Model shows lag in reacting to recent low prices — e.g., when true outcome drops below 60, model still holds forecasts above 65–70 for several days.
- Model tends to overfit recent high prices, leading to “false momentum” in forecasts — e.g., if price recently hit 80, model often forecasts 75–85 for next period, ignoring prior mean.
- Model underestimates the impact of policy or market shocks — e.g., after a regulatory change or auction, model doesn’t adjust downward quickly enough.
- Model exhibits “sticky” behavior — forecasts don’t revert to historical mean quickly after a spike or drop, leading to persistent bias.
- Model often fails to account for “tail risk” — i.e., extreme drops (e.g., below 55) are underpredicted, and model doesn’t adjust for sudden volatility.
- Model tends to overestimate short-term volatility and underpredict long-term mean reversion — e.g., forecasts show sharp swings but don’t settle near historical average within 15–20 days.
